title: Three Ways to Say ER
kidRule: E-R, I-R, and U-R can all make the very same 'er' sound! Your ears cannot tell them apart, so you have to remember which one each word uses. At the end of a longer word it is most often E-R.
hint: Listen for the 'er' sound. Three different vowels can team up with R to make it. Picture the word in your mind: which vowel does this one use?
reminder: The 'er' sound has three spellings: E-R, I-R, and U-R. If one did not work, try another one!

check.question: Why can't we just listen to know which vowel is in THIRTEEN?
check.correctAnswer: Because E-R, I-R, and U-R all sound exactly the same!
distractors: Because THIRTEEN has no vowel sound in it at all
Because I-R is the only way to spell that sound

words.def: The number that is one more than twelve.
words.sent: There are thirteen candles on my cousin's cake.
words.story: A baker's dozen means thirteen. Long ago, bakers added one extra loaf so nobody could say they had sold too little!
words.card: My goldfish turned *thirteen* and became a grumpy *teen*!

words.def: To come back, or to bring something back.
words.sent: Please return the library books by Friday.
words.story: Arctic terns fly from the top of the world to the bottom and then return every single year, the longest trip of any bird!
words.card: It is my *turn* to *return* the dragon to the pet store!

words.def: Someone who chooses to live all alone, far away from other people.
words.sent: The old hermit lived in a cabin deep in the woods.
words.story: A hermit crab does not grow its own shell. It borrows an empty one and moves to a bigger one as it grows!
words.card: The *hermit* crab told *her* mom she was moving into a teapot!

words.def: A traveling show with acrobats, clowns, and jugglers, often in a big tent.
words.sent: An acrobat flipped through the air at the circus.
words.story: This word comes from a Latin word for circle, because the show happens in a round ring!
words.card: Come with *us* to the *circus*, where the elephants juggle peanuts!

words.def: Strong and not easy to break or knock over.
words.sent: We built a sturdy table out of thick planks.
words.story: An eggshell is more sturdy than it looks. Its curved shape spreads out the push, so it is very hard to crush an egg by squeezing its two ends!
words.card: *Stu* the ant built a *sturdy* bridge out of dry noodles!

words.def: Someone who knows a lot about one thing or is very good at it.
words.sent: My aunt is an expert on frogs and toads.
words.story: Some chess experts can play many games at the same time while wearing a blindfold, keeping every board in their heads!
words.card: My *ex*tra clever grandpa is an *expert* at finding lost socks!

words.sent: I was so thirsty after the long race.
words.story: A thirsty camel can drink about 30 gallons of water in less than 15 minutes!
words.card: The *thirsty* pig sipped lemonade in her tidy *sty*!

words.def: A round white and purple vegetable that grows under the ground.
words.sent: Grandpa pulled a giant turnip out of the soil.
words.story: Long before pumpkins were used, people in Ireland carved spooky Halloween faces into turnips!
words.card: It is my *turn* to juggle the giant *turnip*!

words.def: So good that it has no mistakes at all.
words.sent: She did a perfect cartwheel on the grass.
words.story: In bowling, a perfect game means knocking down every pin twelve times in a row, for a score of 300!
words.card: Sup*per* was *perfect* until the dog sat in the soup!

words.def: Awake and busy at night, and asleep during the day.
words.sent: Owls are nocturnal, so they hunt after dark.
words.story: Many nocturnal animals have a shiny layer at the back of their eyes that helps them see in the dark. It is why a cat's eyes glow in a flashlight beam!
words.card: At night it is the *nocturnal* owl's *turn* to use the playground!
